tools_if_shown.name: list_projects
tools_if_shown.description: List the user's Flow projects — the top-level containers holding whiteboards, documents and tactics. Returns id, uid, title, status, the user's role, and created_by_you: false means someone else made this project and shared it, so what is on it is mostly THEIR work, not the user's. Use a project uid with other tools to drill in. Order by 'viewed' to see what they actually work on; the default 'created' is newest-made first, which for a long-standing account is mostly the projects they opened once.

tools_if_shown.name: get_project
tools_if_shown.description: Fetch a single project by uid, including title, status and the user's permission level.

tools_if_shown.name: list_boards
tools_if_shown.description: List a project's boards as a tree: each folder's board with its name, uid (pass it as whiteboard_uid), parent board and the folder element that opens it. Names only; read a board's content with get_whiteboard_elements and its whiteboard_uid.

tools_if_shown.name: get_board_people
tools_if_shown.description: List the people who have access to this board — the same roster the assignee picker shows. Use it to answer 'who is on this board', and before filling a table's person column when the user did not name someone exactly. Returns each person's id and name; a person cell is written with the NAME.

tools_if_shown.name: get_whiteboard
tools_if_shown.description: Fetch a whiteboard's metadata by the owning project id (and optionally the board uid; omit it for the project's root board). Board-level metadata only — use get_whiteboard_elements for the actual content.

tools_if_shown.name: get_whiteboard_elements
tools_if_shown.description: Read what is on a board, with the real text of each element: notes, todos, headings, tickets, tables, documents, tactics, frames and walls. Pass element_uids to read specific elements, or parent_uid to read inside one wall, kanban, group or frame; otherwise the whole board. Containers include their children. An element someone else wrote is marked createdByYou: false.

tools_if_shown.name: get_whiteboard_edges
tools_if_shown.description: Read a board's edges: the arrows and connections between its elements, with their text.

tools_if_shown.name: list_documents
tools_if_shown.description: List the user's documents. scope: 'project' (requires project_uid), 'private', 'shared', or 'recent'. Returns summaries; use get_document for full content.

tools_if_shown.name: get_document
tools_if_shown.description: Fetch a document by uid: title, content and notes. The content HTML carries data-block-id attributes — those are what the edit tools target, so read the document before editing it. The uid in a table's document CELL (inside its tableData payload) is a valid uid here — that is how you read what a cell's document actually says.

tools_if_shown.name: get_tactic
tools_if_shown.description: Fetch a tactic (blueprint) by uid — an expert framework of ordered flip-cards, possibly with a document view. Use get_tactic_cards to read its cards.

tools_if_shown.name: get_tactic_cards
tools_if_shown.description: Read the cards of a tactic (blueprint) by its numeric blueprint id, in display order.

tools_if_shown.name: list_tactics
tools_if_shown.description: Search the tactic LIBRARY — the published expert frameworks a user can attach or start from. Use this to find a tactic by name. Different from get_tactic, which reads a tactic already living inside a project.

tools_if_shown.name: get_tactic_template_cards
tools_if_shown.description: Read the cards of a tactic from the LIBRARY, in display order — each card's title, subtitle and body are the steps of the framework. This is the tool to call for a tactic the user ATTACHED to their message.

tools_if_shown.name: get_board_summary
tools_if_shown.description: An index of what is on a whiteboard — element counts by type, the names of its walls and folders, and the titles of what they hold — without reading every element's content. Use this FIRST for any board the user attached, and for any board you are deciding whether to read. Use get_whiteboard_elements instead once you know you need the actual content. It also reports authorship — how much of what was read the user wrote themselves.

tools_if_shown.name: get_board_layout
tools_if_shown.description: The board's real geometry: every element's position and the size the canvas actually draws it at (stored sizes are not real — notes fit their text, walls grow with their cards, documents draw as large cards). Positions are absolute board coordinates; a wall's cards come with parent_uid and their place inside the wall. Use it before placing, aligning or resizing things relative to what is already there. Each element says whether its box was measured or estimated. A board that changed since its last measure takes a few seconds to measure. Returns at most 500 elements, top to bottom, and says so in `note` when a board holds more.

tools_if_shown.name: get_board_changes
tools_if_shown.description: What HAPPENED on this board — per card: created, edited, moved, refiled (into or out of a wall), restyled or deleted, who did it, when, and whether it was your own earlier work in this chat. Answers 'what changed?', 'what did I do here since last time?', 'how has this board evolved?'. Default window is since your last turn in this chat. Not a board read: it says what changed, not what is there — read the board itself with get_board_summary or get_whiteboard_elements.

tools_if_shown.name: get_deleted_elements
tools_if_shown.description: What is in this board's trash: everything deleted from it in the last 7 days, split into what the user deleted and what others deleted. Each entry carries the history_id that restore_deleted_elements needs — element uids do not restore anything. Use it when the user says something was deleted, lost or went missing from a board. Only board elements have a trash: a deleted project, document or gallery upload is gone for good, so say that instead of searching for it.

tools_if_shown.name: read_file
tools_if_shown.description: Read the text of a FILE on the board (PDF, DOCX, XLSX, XLS, CSV, TXT, MD, code…) and return its contents. Use this BEFORE answering anything about a file — summarising it, pulling its rows into a table, turning it into tasks or a shotlist. A board read gives you only the file's name and address; its contents come from here. Never answer from a filename. Long files come back truncated, and the result says so.

tools_if_shown.name: create_whiteboard_element
tools_if_shown.description:
Create ONE element on a whiteboard and return its uid. This is the only way to put anything on a board. Each call is one element, and every call whose inputs you already have goes in the SAME step: they land one after another in the order you write them, so the user still watches the board fill, and each step you do not take is one less re-read of the whole prompt. Wait for the next step only for a call that needs a uid another call returns.

Compose whatever structure fits. A new wall and its cards are ONE build_section call; here, a card for a wall that already exists takes parent_uid set to that wall's uid. On a board that has walls, a folder, document or note goes in one; only a title note (background_color "transparent"), a picture or a shape sits loose.

Position and size are decided for you so nothing overlaps — there is no geometry to pass. Creates are immediate and not reviewed; the user can undo.

A CHECKLIST IS ONE CARD: for a to-do list, make a single todo call with every task on its own line in `text`. Each line becomes a checkbox on that one card. A separate card per task is not a list, even when earlier turns in this conversation or cards already on the board look like that.

NOT for changing something that already exists. Adding detail to, expanding, or rewriting an existing element is update_element on THAT element — never a new element beside it holding the addition, even if the board or earlier turns already show that pattern.

tools_if_shown.name: add_document_to_board
tools_if_shown.description: Put an EXISTING document on the board — the one the user attached, or one you found with list_documents. Use this whenever they ask to add/put/place a document they already have onto the board. Do NOT use create_whiteboard_element with type 'document' for this: that makes a NEW blank document instead of showing theirs. The document may live in another project; pass only its uid.

tools_if_shown.name: connect_whiteboard_elements
tools_if_shown.description:
Draw an arrow between two elements on a board, to show flow or relationship. Both uids must be elements you have seen via get_whiteboard_elements. Connecting two walls standing side by side also widens the gap between them, so the line and any text on it have room.
The read gave you both elements' positions, so USE THEM: an element sitting BELOW another is joined bottom to top, and leaving the default right-to-left there draws a line that loops around the outside of its own card before it arrives.

tools_if_shown.name: build_section
tools_if_shown.description:
Build one section of a board in one call: a wall and every card inside it, top to bottom, written in the order given. Send every section of a board this way; create_whiteboard_element is for loose items and for adding to a wall that already exists.

A card takes the fields of create_whiteboard_element (type, title, text, table columns and rows, labels) except parent_uid, after_uid, frame_uid, project_uid and whiteboard_uid, and is never a wall. Give the wall a width when a card is a table. A document's card may carry its opening section in text.

A card that fails leaves the others in place: the result lists each card's uid or error, so resend only a failed card with create_whiteboard_element and after_uid set to the card above it. A folder's contents go in a later call with whiteboard_uid set to the folder's board, from list_boards.

tools_if_shown.name: update_element
tools_if_shown.description: Update an EXISTING element in place: its content and/or its styling. Applies immediately, exactly like the user editing on the canvas, and the user can undo it. content: for a note, todo or heading pass the full replacement text, markdown or HTML; for a ticket pass an object with the fields to change (title, description, label, labelColorHex, date); for other types pass an object patching the content keys you saw in get_whiteboard_elements A FOLDER takes {boardName} to rename it, {iconName} to change its icon and {iconColorHex} for its colour — for those two pass a WORD, not a hex or an icon name: iconName is one of [research, idea, strategy, planning, tasks, notes, meeting, launch, archive, inbox, templates, settings, design, writing, brand, photo, video, music, audio, marketing, sales, finance, budget, invoice, analytics, legal, clients, team, support, product, shop, engineering, bugs, security, data, cloud, travel, food, health, fitness, home, education, science, nature, mountain, camping, weather, transport, gear, events, gifts, reading, location, global, favourites, important, private, time, folder] and iconColorHex is one of [tan, blue, rose, purple, steel, brown, red, navy, violet, slate, coral, orange] (either can be 'none' to clear it), and {coverImage} to put a PICTURE on the tile instead of an icon — that is what a folder's cover image or thumbnail is. coverImage takes a stored image key (a board image's imageUrl, a generated image's image_url, or a gallery key), never a web url; 'none' clears it back to a plain tile. A folder shows a picture or an icon, never both, so setting iconName on a folder that has a cover replaces the picture. Changing only the colour leaves the icon or cover exactly as it is. An IMAGE (or AI image) takes {caption} — the line shown UNDER the picture, which is what "caption this" or "write a caption" means; a bare string is read as the caption too. An empty caption hides the caption row, and {showCaption: false} hides a caption while keeping its text. Nothing else about an image is edited here: its url, crop and source images are refused. Captions are not labels — labels are the parameter below. A TABLE is the one fiddly case: pass {tableData: "<json STRING>"} — tableData is stringified JSON, not an object — shaped {id, type:'table', data:{name, columns:[{id,name,type}], columnOrder:[id], rows:[{id, values:{<columnId>: cell}}], rowOrder:[id]}}. Keep the ids of everything you are not changing. Adding a column means appending to BOTH columns and columnOrder and adding that column's id to EVERY row's values; removing one means deleting it from all three; reordering means reordering columnOrder or rowOrder alone. Send the WHOLE table back, not a fragment. A column may also carry cellType ('number'|'currency'|'percent'|'datetime'|'duration'|'checkbox'|'rating'|'labels'|'status'|'person'|'url'|'email'|'phone'), width (px), icon (its header glyph) and, on a currency column, currency (an ISO code like 'EUR' picking the symbol its cells render in — the cells hold a bare number either way). data itself carries the table's own heading: title (the name shown ABOVE the grid), description (the caption under it) and icon (the glyph beside the title, a WORD from the same list as a column's). Renaming a table means changing data.title — data.name is the payload's internal label and is invisible on the canvas. PRESERVE every such field you are not deliberately changing, or you will silently reset the user's column types, widths, icons, captions and the table's own name. A column's icon is normally left off entirely, because the canvas derives one from the column's NAME — so renaming a column is usually all it takes to change its icon. To pin a specific one, set icon to a WORD from [name, title, owner, assignee, person, team, client, company, audience, character, identity, personality, background, relationship, story, status, stage, progress, priority, approval, done, task, checklist, type, category, tags, topic, platform, channel, date, deadline, schedule, calendar, duration, time, count, quantity, id, budget, cost, price, revenue, invoice, payment, percent, score, rating, metrics, data, notes, description, video, image, photo, audio, file, document, attachment, link, email, phone, comment, message, location, country, address, travel, campaign, marketing, sales, product, keyword, views, engagement, goal, launch, project, shop, discount, code, bug, security, version, book, education, language, weather, home, vehicle, important, private, archive, settings, idea, edit]; an unrecognised word is dropped and the name is used instead. Typed cells are written as WORDS and resolved here, so write what you mean and let the column hold it: a labels cell is its tags comma-separated ('Introductory, Technical classic'), a person cell the assignees' names, a status cell one of (Not started, Blocked, In progress, In review, Done, Archived), a rating a number 0-5, a checkbox 'true'/'false', a datetime 'YYYY-MM-DD', a duration what was typed ('1:30'). Labels are matched against the user's own palette and created when they are new; names are matched against this board's members. A cell you are not changing can be copied through in whatever form you were shown it. A column that cannot honour one of its values — a name nobody on the board has, a word that is not one of the stages — becomes a plain TEXT column so the words still show, so pick the cellType that fits what you are actually writing. attributes: patch using the canvas's OWN key names — backgroundColor, topBarHighlightColor (that is the accent stripe, NOT 'highlightColor'), width, height, borderColor, fontSize, textAlign. backgroundColor 'transparent' on a note or todo takes its card away and leaves the text on the canvas, which is what turns one into a title; '' puts the card back. labels: the element's complete new chip label set — it REPLACES what is there, so send the labels you are keeping too, and an empty array clears them. Notes and todos take 8; images, AI images, colours, files, videos and walls take 4, the same limit the canvas's label menu enforces. Nothing else takes chip labels: a ticket's single label is part of its content. Documents are edited with the document tools, never here; a deck's content with update_deck and a design page's html or name with update_html_app.

tools_if_shown.name: move_element
tools_if_shown.description: Move an EXISTING element: into a wall (parent_uid + parent_order_index), out of a wall (parent_uid: '' plus a canvas location), reordering within a wall, or repositioning any element (location only, in board coordinates). Frame membership follows the destination on its own — land inside a frame to join it, outside to leave it. Applies immediately, like the user dragging it; the user can undo.

tools_if_shown.name: set_connection_text
tools_if_shown.description: Change the text riding on arrows already on the board, or clear it with an empty string. This is the answer to 'put the durations on those arrows' or 'make that one 6 weeks'. Do NOT delete the arrow and draw a new one: redrawing loses the curve the user dragged into it and gives the connection a new uid. edge uids come from get_whiteboard_edges or connect_whiteboard_elements' result — element uids are not edge uids.

tools_if_shown.name: create_chart
tools_if_shown.description:
Create ONE native chart element (bar, line or pie) on the board. Data and styling live in the element; the canvas renders it as a real interactive chart. Use real values only — never invented numbers. This is the RIGHT answer to most requests to chart something: one fact is one chart, and the same measure across several categories is this tool called once per category (small multiples read better than one crowded chart). Reach for create_dashboard only when the ask is an overview of several different measures. ALWAYS send value_format when the values are money or percentages — without it they render as bare numbers — and add a caption saying what the chart shows whenever you have a finding worth stating.

BUILDING FROM A PICTURE THE USER PASTED: what carries across is the DATA, the category and series names, the chart type, the bar direction and the series colours. Nothing else does — the background, typography, gridlines, spacing and legend placement are the canvas's own and are not settable here. So say what you actually matched. Announcing a chart as being in "the same style" beside a screenshot it visibly does not resemble is the one claim the user checks immediately, and it costs you the ones they cannot check.

tools_if_shown.name: create_dashboard
tools_if_shown.description: Create a whole dashboard: chart tiles laid out in a justified grid the tool computes. You design WHICH tiles share a row and their relative spans; the tool owns the pixels. Rows render top to bottom; a good dashboard opens with a row of 3-4 metric tiles, then chart rows of 1-3 tiles. Max 16 tiles. Real values only. USE IT WHEN THE ASK IS AN OVERVIEW — a dashboard, a report, a summary, 'how are we doing' — or when four or more different measures are worth showing at once. A request for a chart, a graph or a picture of ONE thing is create_chart, not a grid with that chart buried in it. Never invent a tile to fill the grid: if the data holds four things worth showing, the dashboard is four tiles. ALWAYS send value_format on tiles whose values are money or percentages, and give a gauge its real value_min/value_max (NPS runs -100 to 100) — the ring is drawn against 0-100 otherwise and is wrong.

tools_if_shown.name: update_chart
tools_if_shown.description: Change a chart that is ALREADY on the board — its data, its title, or how it is drawn. This is a patch: send only what changes and the rest of the chart is kept, so "make it horizontal" is {layout: "horizontal"} and nothing else. Use it instead of building a replacement whenever the chart is nearly right — the user keeps its place, size and the undo history that goes with it. It applies immediately and the user can undo it. A chart's TYPE cannot change here (a bar chart cannot become a line chart): that is a create plus a delete of the old one.

tools_if_shown.name: create_diagram
tools_if_shown.description:
Draw a DIAGRAM in one call — a flowchart, a user journey, an org chart, a swimlane, a state machine, a process: boxes on a grid with labelled arrows between them. Use this whenever the shape of the answer is boxes-and-arrows, however the user said it ('map the signup flow', 'how does a ticket move through support', 'chart our approval process').

It CANNOT be built one element at a time. Free placement answers 'somewhere free' rather than 'column 2, row 3', so the boxes step diagonally across the canvas and the arrows between them mean nothing. Here you say which CELL each node is in and the tool owns every coordinate: one width for every box, a column as wide as its widest node, and the space a labelled arrow needs bought out of the boundary it crosses so no chip lands on a box.

Use create_mindmap for a centre with branches radiating off it, create_constellation for a web of notes with sub-branches, and create_orbit for one ring of small things around a hub. This is the one for a flow that goes somewhere.

This builds BOARD ELEMENTS the user keeps working on. When they want ONE finished thing to take away instead — a timeline, framework or explainer to screenshot into a deck, show a client or send — that is create_html_app, which lays the same material out as a single designed page.

tools_if_shown.name: create_mindmap
tools_if_shown.description:
Create a whole mind map in one call: a central topic, branches and sub-branches, laid out and colored by the tool with connecting edges. You supply ONLY the content tree; never create mindmap notes or edges yourself. Node text is concise (3-8 words).

A NODE HOLDS 3-8 WORDS, so a request that names the SECTIONS it wants — premise, acts, characters, themes, arcs — is asking for a board of walls it can write paragraphs in, and the word "map" in it does not make it a mind map. Build those with walls and cards; reach here for a branching tree of short labels, or when they ask for a mind map by name.

THERE IS NO EXTEND. This always builds a WHOLE map, so "add more to this mind map" means deleting the one that is there and putting a replacement in its place — which costs every node the user dragged, and anything they attached to the old nodes. Ask before doing that, and if you do it, say it was REBUILT. Reporting a replacement as an expansion ("expanded the mindmap, keeping the same three branches") is a claim the layout itself contradicts the moment they look at it.

tools_if_shown.name: create_constellation
tools_if_shown.description: Create a whole constellation in one call: a radial web of rich notes (a central idea, themes, sub-notes) laid out and connected by the tool. You supply ONLY the content tree; never create constellation notes or edges yourself. 20-35 nodes make a good constellation; node text can be a sentence or two.

tools_if_shown.name: create_orbit
tools_if_shown.description:
Create an ORBIT in one call: a small central label with things ringed around it and a curved line drawn from the centre out to each one. ANY mix of cards can ring the hub — pictures, colour swatches, notes, links, videos, tickets, checklists, documents and folders — so this is the shape for 'everything about X in one place', as well as the film colour palette and inspiration wall the boards we ship use it for. It CANNOT be built by creating the pieces one at a time: free placement steps them diagonally across the canvas and nothing joins them up. Supply only the centre and the members; the tool owns every coordinate, the ring radius and every line.
Use create_color_palette instead when the user wants a plain palette block (a grid of swatches, no hub, no lines) — that is the commoner request. Use create_constellation for a web of substantial NOTES with sub-branches; an orbit is ONE ring of small things.

tools_if_shown.name: create_color_palette
tools_if_shown.description: Put a COLOUR PALETTE on the board: several swatches laid out as a grid, in ONE call. This is how a palette is built — never several create_whiteboard_element calls with type 'color', which cannot make a grid and leaves the swatches in one long row running off the canvas. Each swatch shows its colour, the name you give it, and its hex and RGB values (those two are rendered from the hex, so do not write them into the name). Use it whenever the user asks for a palette, colour scheme, brand colours or swatches — including when you are reading the colours off a picture they attached. The swatches sit loose on the canvas as a block; to put colours INSIDE a wall instead, use create_whiteboard_element with a parent_uid.

tools_if_shown.name: divide_board_sections
tools_if_shown.description:
Draw a LINE between groups of content so the board reads as separate sections — the vertical rule between a personal column and the team's columns, the line under a header row. Name what sits on each side and the line is measured and drawn for you: the sections are slid apart to make room, and the rule runs down the middle of that space, the height of the tallest thing it divides.
Use it when the user asks to divide, split or separate parts of a board, and when a board YOU have just built has two runs of content that belong to different people, time ranges or stages — a divider is what says they are different rather than a long row of walls.
Call it LAST, after everything it separates is on the board: it measures what is actually there, so a wall created afterwards lands on the wrong side of the line. Name the WALLS and other top-level elements, never the cards inside a wall.

tools_if_shown.name: create_shot_cards
tools_if_shown.description: Build a shot list in the CARD format — a connected left-to-right row of shot walls, each holding its frame, a chips note, a 'Shots required' checklist, a scene-direction note and an equipment note, with an arrow to the next shot. Use this INSTEAD of many create_whiteboard_element calls whenever you are building shot cards: it is one call for the whole row, so a 20- or 40-shot list actually finishes. You supply the content of every shot; the tool owns the walls, card order, colours and arrows. Pass EVERY shot the user asked for in one call. WHEN THE PICTURES ARE ALREADY ON THE BOARD — selected, or asked for in words — pass each one's uid as that shot's image_element_uid in THIS call, so their own pictures become the frames. Moving them in after the call instead leaves the empty placeholder frame this tool built standing in every wall beside them. Never leave a selected picture without a shot.

tools_if_shown.name: create_strip_board
tools_if_shown.description: Build a strip board — the shooting schedule — in ONE call: a wall per shoot day, a coloured strip per scene, in shooting order, each day totalled in pages and chained to the next by an arrow. Use this INSTEAD of individual create_whiteboard_element calls for any strip board or shooting schedule: pass EVERY day and every strip at once. Strip colours are the industry code (INT/EXT × day/night) and the tool sets them — never colour a strip yourself. Take scenes, page counts and cast from the script's SCENE INDEX (read_script_scenes) or the scene table on the board, never from memory of the prose.

tools_if_shown.name: create_deck
tools_if_shown.description:
Put a DECK on the board: one element that shows one slide at a time, with every slide created under it. Each slide is a self-contained static HTML page at the deck's fixed slide size, written against the deck theme's CSS variables (--deck-bg, --deck-fg, --deck-accent, --deck-muted, --deck-font, --deck-scale) so one theme change re-skins every slide. The same hard constraints as create_html_app apply to every slide: no scripts, no external URLs, pictures as empty data-image-slot elements named in image_slots. The user edits slides by hand afterwards, presents the deck fullscreen and exports it as one PDF.
This is what a request for SLIDES builds — a pitch deck, a treatment, a lookbook, "a ten-page treatment" — not the PDF tools, which compose a file (ADR-0112). A social CAROUSEL post (Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok slides) is not a deck: create_carousel_pages (ADR-0118). A shot list asked for by name is the card row create_shot_cards builds; only the design-shot-list workflow wants it as a deck.
A deck already on the board does not make a request an edit; what the user asked for decides. Asked to change THAT deck ("the deck", "my deck", "this slide", "it", add, remove or reorder slides, re-theme it): change it with update_html_app per slide, add_deck_slides, remove_deck_slides, reorder_deck_slides, update_deck for the theme, and never build a second deck beside one the user asked you to alter. Asked for A deck ("a new pitch deck", "another deck", "a deck from these images"): this tool, and the deck already there is left exactly as it is: none of its slides rewritten, filled or removed. Only a whole-deck redo that could mean either ("redo the pitch deck with these pictures") gets one question first, even though it names the deck: change the deck on the board, or build a new one beside it.
Pictures the user attached to their message go into the slides with fill_image_slot, not onto the board on their own.

tools_if_shown.name: update_deck
tools_if_shown.description: Change a deck that is already on the board: its title, its aspect, or any part of its theme. A PATCH — pass only what changes, because the palette, font and type scale the user set by hand are all in here and sending the ones you did not mean to touch resets them. Re-theming re-skins every slide at once; you never rewrite slides to change a colour.

tools_if_shown.name: add_deck_slides
tools_if_shown.description: Add slides to a deck that already exists, written against the same theme variables as the rest (--deck-bg, --deck-fg, --deck-accent, --deck-muted, --deck-font, --deck-scale). Use this to grow a deck the user asked to extend; never build a second deck beside the first. A request for a new or another deck is create_deck, never slides added to this one.

tools_if_shown.name: remove_deck_slides
tools_if_shown.description: Delete slides from a deck by uid and close the gap in the order. A deck has to keep at least one slide; to get rid of a whole deck, delete the deck element itself.

tools_if_shown.name: reorder_deck_slides
tools_if_shown.description: Put a deck's slides in a new order. Pass EVERY slide uid, in the order you want them — a partial list is refused rather than guessed at.

tools_if_shown.name: create_carousel_pages
tools_if_shown.description: Put a social CAROUSEL POST on the board: every slide as its own design page, laid out left to right in slide order, all at the post's fixed size. This is what "carousel posts", "a swipe post", "slides for Instagram / LinkedIn / TikTok" build — never create_deck, whose slides live inside one element and move with it. Once placed, the pages are independent: the user drags, deletes or edits any one alone, and update_html_app rewrites one. Each page is a self-contained static HTML document under the same constraints as create_html_app: no scripts, no external URLs, pictures as empty data-image-slot elements named in image_slots.

tools_if_shown.name: find_board_template
tools_if_shown.description: Search the board templates this app ships (Film Plan, Shotlist, Storyboard, Agency Hub, Moodboard, Second Brain and dozens more) and get back their names and uids. Use it when the user names a template, or when a request matches a board we already have a good shape for and starting from it beats building the shape from nothing. Returns candidates only — picking one and applying it is apply_board_template.

tools_if_shown.name: apply_board_template
tools_if_shown.description:
Put a whole shipped template onto the board the user is on, in one go, with its exact layout — every wall, card, colour and connection where the template puts them. Then it reads the board back and returns an inventory of what landed, with a uid for every element, so you can rewrite the cards for THIS user's subject with update_element.
The template arrives carrying its own worked example (Film Plan ships a North Face climbing commercial). That content is a starting point to REPLACE, not to leave: after applying, work through the inventory and rewrite every card that names the example's subject. Leaving it is worse than never applying, because the user is handed a stranger's production.
Only apply when the user asked for that template, or agreed to start from it. Never apply one speculatively onto a board that already has their work on it.

tools_if_shown.name: write_document_content
tools_if_shown.description: Append to (or replace) the contents of a document by uid. Use this to fill a document you created on a board, one section per call, so it builds up rather than arriving all at once. For the document currently open on screen, use the editing tools instead.

tools_if_shown.name: set_document_cover
tools_if_shown.description:
Give a document an icon and a banner image, the way a person would from the document header. Do this for documents YOU create — not for one the user made and you only edited.

icon takes a TOPIC WORD, not an icon name: research, idea, strategy, planning, tasks, notes, meeting, launch, archive, inbox, templates, settings, design, writing, brand, photo, video, music, audio, marketing, sales, finance, budget, invoice, analytics, legal, clients, team, support, product, shop, engineering, bugs, security, data, cloud, travel, food, health, fitness, home, education, science, nature, mountain, camping, weather, transport, gear, events, gifts, reading, location, global, favourites, important, private, time, folder. A word outside that list sets no icon and tells you so. It also accepts a stored image key to use a picture as the icon.

banner takes 'gradient' for one of the app's own gradients (free, and the right answer unless the subject genuinely wants a photograph), or a stored image key from find_document_images or generate_document_image. A url from the open web is refused: a cover comes from the same places the user's own picker offers.

tools_if_shown.name: convert_notes_to_documents
tools_if_shown.description: Move whole notes into documents, keeping their text exactly as written. Use this whenever a note is long enough to be a document — roughly a screenful or more — and whenever the user asks for documents. NEVER retype a note's content into a new document yourself: that is slow, it risks dropping their words, and this does it as a move. The originals are deleted in the same undo step, so the board is left holding the documents and not both. Give wall_uid to file them into a wall you have already created.

tools_if_shown.name: create_document_in_table_cell
tools_if_shown.description: Create a project document and put it in one cell of a table's document column, so that cell opens the document. Use for 'give every episode an outline', 'add a script to each scene'. The cell shows the document's own name and icon — do NOT also write the title into a text cell. Fill the document afterwards with write_document_content, passing the returned document_uid and NO element_uid.

tools_if_shown.name: put_document_in_table_cell
tools_if_shown.description: Point a cell of a table's document column at a project document that already exists. Find candidates with list_documents. To create a new one instead, use create_document_in_table_cell.

tools_if_shown.name: clear_document_from_table_cell
tools_if_shown.description: Empty a cell of a table's document column. The document itself is NOT deleted — it stays in the project's documents and can be put back.

tools_if_shown.name: group_into_walls
tools_if_shown.description:
Rehouse elements that are ALREADY on the board into walls — the whole plan in ONE call. Each group either makes a new wall (title) or files into a wall already there (wall_uid), and the elements are MOVED, so the user keeps the cards they wrote and the board holds no copies.

This is how a board gets organized. Never do it as a run of create_whiteboard_element + move_element calls: fifty cards is fifty round trips, the user watches it crawl, and a turn that runs out of room leaves the board half sorted. A new wall joins the board's wall row, or — on a board with no walls yet — lands beside the material it holds. Every write shares this turn's single undo step.

It moves elements and names walls. It never writes, rewrites or splits what the user wrote.

The receipt carries `still_loose`: how many fileable cards are STILL on the canvas after your plan ran. Cards you meant to leave out are in that number too, so read it against what you intended — if it is higher than that, the plan missed cards and a second call files them.

tools_if_shown.name: add_images
tools_if_shown.description:
Put pictures you already have the addresses of onto the board: photos from your own web search, images on a page the user shared, links the user pasted. Storyflow downloads each one and keeps its own copy in the user's gallery, so it stays on the board after the link dies. Pass the image file's own address (ends in .jpg, .png, .webp or serves an image), not the page it sits on.

BY DEFAULT IT PLACES THE PICTURES ITSELF, loose or inside parent_uid; do not create image elements for them afterwards. To fill an EMPTY image frame already on the board, pass one image and its target_uid. When the pictures go into something you build (deck slides, orbit members, shot-card frames, one picture per wall across several walls), pass place_on_board: false and use the image_url values it returns.

Only use addresses you actually found or were given, never invented ones. An address that could not be stored comes back in `missing`: say which, and offer to try another link.

tools_if_shown.name: create_project
tools_if_shown.description: Create a new, empty Storyflow project with the given title, the same way the app's New project button does: it comes with its root board. Returns the new project's uid; pass it as project_uid to the board and document tools to fill it in. Use only when the user asks for a new project.

tools_if_shown.name: request_photo_upload
tools_if_shown.description: A picture the user attached in this chat never reaches Storyflow: you see it, Storyflow cannot. Call this to let them put pictures from their phone or computer on a board in one tap. It returns a link good for 15 minutes; put it in your reply as a link whose text is "Add your photos". The user taps it, picks any number of pictures, and each one lands on the board as it uploads, visible in the board card and in Storyflow. Pass target_uids for empty frames you placed for them, or parent_uid for the wall the pictures belong in; with neither, a wall is made for them when the first picture arrives. Never tell the user Storyflow cannot take their photo, and never ask them to upload inside Storyflow.

tools_if_shown.name: search
tools_if_shown.description: Search the user's Storyflow projects, boards and documents by title. Returns ids for fetch: project:<uid>, board:<project_uid>/<whiteboard_uid>, document:<project_uid>/<uid>.

tools_if_shown.name: fetch
tools_if_shown.description: Fetch one record by an id returned from search: a project, a board's elements or a document.

detail_provenance.offline_parser_correction: Decoded escaped leading dollar literals and omitted Flight undefined properties; original HTML hash/timestamp retained.

published_auth_text: stripe-mcp requires authentication. Connect it in Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor and complete the OAuth login prompt.

published_tools.source: published FAQ (same names as visible imported tool chips)

tools_if_shown.name: stripe_implementation_planner
tools_if_shown.description:
Stripe integration planner. Use this tool to help users accept payments, sell products online, set up billing, set up a marketplace or platform, or build any Stripe integration. Call this BEFORE writing code when the user wants to charge customers, add a checkout flow, handle subscriptions, create invoices, or monetize their app.

WHEN TO USE:
  Call this tool when the user wants to:
  - Accept payments, take payments, or charge customers (credit cards, bank transfers, wallets)
  - Sell online, build e-commerce, add a shopping cart, or create a checkout page
  - Set up subscriptions, recurring billing, metered billing, or usage-based pricing
  - Send invoices or collect one-time payments
  - Add Stripe to their app, integrate Stripe, or build a payment flow
  - Understand which Stripe products to use (Checkout, Elements, Payment Intents, Connect, Billing)
  - Plan an integration architecture before writing code
  - Monetize an app, add billing, or start charging users

FIRST CALL GUIDANCE:
  Ask the user about their business and payment requirements before choosing a use case:
  - What do they sell? (physical goods, digital products, SaaS, services, marketplace)
  - Payment model? (one-time, subscriptions, invoices, usage-based)
  - Platform? (web, mobile app, in-person, payment links)
  - Complexity? (simple payment link vs. custom integration in existing tech stack)
  Then pass their full description as the message parameter.

Returns JSON with use cases, decision trees, documentation links, and a guide_id for follow-up calls.

RULES:
  - Do NOT pass a guide_id unless you received it from this tool in this conversation.
  - Do NOT retry with different guide_ids if one fails — omit guide_id to start fresh.

tools_if_shown.name: send_stripe_feedback
tools_if_shown.description:
Share feedback about Stripe's products.

Submit when the user gives product feedback or you observe something concrete that worked or failed. Do not report model behavior, the user's local environment, an unclear prompt, or a recovered tool error.

Use actor "human" for the user's own words; "agent" for your observations. Not a support channel — no ticket or reply.

tools_if_shown.name: search_stripe_documentation
tools_if_shown.description:
Search the Stripe documentation for the given question and language.

It takes two arguments:
- question (str): The user question to search an answer for in the Stripe documentation.
- language (str, optional): The programming language to search for in the documentation.

tools_if_shown.name: stripe_api_search
tools_if_shown.description:
Search for Stripe API operations by providing an intent and a resource to operate on.

For the resource, use a specific, descriptive phrase (e.g. "issuing card transactions", "payout methods", "outbound payments") rather than a single generic noun — Stripe has many similar resources, and the extra qualifiers help disambiguate between them rather than causing a miss. Only fall back to the bare core noun (e.g. "transactions") if a specific multi-word search returns no results.

Returns matching operations with their HTTP method, path, summary, and top-level parameter names with types. Does not include parameter descriptions, enum values, or nested object fields — use stripe_api_details to get those before calling the relevant Stripe API execution tool.

tools_if_shown.name: stripe_api_details
tools_if_shown.description:
Get detailed parameter information for a specific Stripe API operation.
Provide the stripe_api_operation_id from stripe_api_search results to see all path, query, and body parameters with their types, descriptions, and whether they are required.

Use before calling the relevant Stripe API execution tool for operations with nested object fields.

The response may include an "LLM Context" section with usage guidance specific to the operation — follow any instructions there.

tools_if_shown.name: stripe_api_read
tools_if_shown.description:
Read data from any Stripe API GET operation:
1. Use stripe_api_search to find the operation ID.
2. Use stripe_api_details to understand its parameters (required for operations with nested object fields like address, metadata, or restrictions).
3. Call this tool with the stripe_api_operation_id and a parameters object containing path and query parameters. For mutations (POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE), use stripe_api_write instead.
Monetary values in responses are in the smallest currency unit (e.g. 1000 = $10.00 USD for most currencies).

tools_if_shown.name: stripe_api_write
tools_if_shown.description:
Write data via any Stripe API POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE operation:
1. Use stripe_api_search to find the operation ID.
2. Use stripe_api_details to understand its parameters (required for operations with nested object fields like address, metadata, or restrictions).
3. Call this tool with the stripe_api_operation_id and a parameters object containing path, query, and body parameters. For read-only lookups (GET), use stripe_api_read instead.
All monetary amounts must be in the smallest currency unit (e.g. 1000 = $10.00 USD for most currencies).

tools_if_shown.name: atlas_company_formation
tools_if_shown.description:
Stripe Atlas: start or resume a Delaware C corp/LLC formation. Set action to:
- "list": check for existing applications before "create", using an authorized account. Returns applications
  the current user can access as primary representative. Show any matches to the user. Applications with
  submitted_at are already submitted; offer to resume only drafts or create a separate company.
- "create": create a new Atlas application, which also creates a new Stripe merchant required for Atlas.
  You can call "create" from a sandbox or testmode account; the new Stripe account is always a live account.
  Follow the returned authorization instructions.
- "retrieve": load the formation and next step on the authorized Atlas account.
- "advance": save step and data. Follow next_step_instructions and next_step_schema; steps can be revisited.

For a chosen merchant_id, get stripe_context from list_available_accounts_or_orgs. That tool checks session
access, not application existence. If the account is missing, authorize it with manage_stripe_accounts and
refresh the account list before retrieving its formation.

Drafts only: submission, signing, payment, and personal tax IDs happen in the Dashboard.
Creation is not idempotent. After a timeout or unclear failure, don't retry "create"; use "list" and "retrieve"
before resending only missing changes using returned IDs.

tools_if_shown.name: stripe_analytics
tools_if_shown.description:
This tool is for analyzing Stripe Sigma and Metrics data (e.g. about revenue, charges, products, invoices, subscriptions, disputes, transactions, tax tables, payments etc) and running SQL-based reporting queries. Use it for historical analytics, aggregations, and business intelligence questions (e.g. MRR, churn, cohorts, revenue trends). Prefer this tool over making multiple Stripe API calls that would need to be joined or aggregated client-side.
## SQL Query Runs

**execute_query_run**: Runs a SQL query (Trino) against reporting tables. Requires `sql`. Returns a QueryRun object; use retrieve_query_run to poll.
**retrieve_query_run**: Retrieves a QueryRun's status and results. Requires `query_run_id`.
**search_query_tables**: Searches available reporting tables by keyword. Requires `search_string`.
**retrieve_query_table**: Gets full schema for a specific table. Requires `table_name`, which is the `name` parameter in each table.
**execute_query_template**: Starts a pre-built query template for subscription/billing metrics (Trino, async). Requires `metric`. Optional: `dimensions`, `grains`, `metric_filters`. Returns a `query_run_id`; use retrieve_query_template to poll for results.
**retrieve_query_template**: Retrieves the status/results of a template run started by execute_query_template. Requires `query_run_id`.

### workflow (custom SQL):
  1. search_query_tables: find relevant tables
  2. retrieve_query_table: get column names and types
  3. execute_query_run: run SQL
  4. retrieve_query_run: poll status, get download link

### workflow (query templates):
  1. execute_query_template: start a template-based metric query (returns a query_run_id)
  2. retrieve_query_template: poll with query_run_id (exponential backoff) until status is 'succeeded', then get download link

## Return types
 All monetary values returned by this tool are expressed in the smallest currency unit. For example:
- 1000 is 10 USD (most two-decimal currencies like GBP, EUR, AUD, CAD, divide by 100 to get the major unit value)
- 10 is 10 JPY (zero-decimal currency)
- 10000 is 10 BHD (three-decimal currency)
- 1000000 is 1 USDC
If you don't know how many decimals are in a currency's minor units, use the search_stripe_documentation tool to look it up in https://docs.stripe.com/currencies#minor-units

tools_if_shown.name: list_available_accounts_or_orgs
tools_if_shown.description:
Lists all Stripe accounts in this session with their stripe_context and livemode values.
- Call this first to get stripe_context and livemode before any account-specific operation.
- After calling, ask the user which account to use unless already specified.
- Warn the user before switching between testmode and livemode.

tools_if_shown.name: manage_stripe_accounts
tools_if_shown.description:
Returns a URL to the Stripe Dashboard where users can add accounts, remove accounts, or change permissions for this session.
- Use when the user wants to add, remove, or modify permissions for an account.
- Call this directly — no need to call list_available_accounts_or_orgs first.
- Present the URL to the user and wait for them to confirm they completed their changes.
- After confirmation, call list_available_accounts_or_orgs to sync the updated account list.

tools_if_shown.name: estimate_taxes

tools_if_shown.name: connect_with_expert

tools_if_shown.name: tax_document_checklist
tools_if_shown.description: Returns a personalized list of tax documents and forms you need to gather before filing your tax return. Based on your income sources, deductions, and life events. Covers W-2s, 1099s, receipts, and other IRS forms. This is for DIY filers preparing their own return.

tools_if_shown.name: ask_tax_question

tools_if_shown.name: find_interview_topic

tools_if_shown.name: tax_deadlines

tools_if_shown.name: get_selling_options

Returns the best way to list for the ticketing company the tickets were bought from (e.g. Ticketmaster, Ticketek, DICE, Eventbrite) and a direct tixel.com link to that listing page, plus generic fallbacks (forwarding the confirmation email, uploading a PDF). Prefer the recommended option; offer fallbacks if the user can't use it (e.g. no account access). Do not use for buying tickets — use search_events instead.

tools_if_shown.description: Begin listing (selling) a user's tickets on Tixel straight from their inbox. Returns a one-off Tixel scanner address (scanAlias). The host should then use its email connector to forward the user's original ticket confirmation email — including any PDF or ticket attachments — to that address, sent from the email account the tickets were bought with so Tixel can verify ownership. After forwarding, call check_listing_status with the returned sessionToken to track parsing and get the link to finish the listing. Use this when the user has a confirmation email or e-tickets and wants to sell them; use get_selling_options instead if they ask how selling works or bought from a ticketing company with a direct Tixel integration (e.g. Ticketmaster, Eventbrite).

tools_if_shown.name: check_listing_status

Long-polls (up to ~25s) while Tixel scans the forwarded email, then returns the parse status, any detected tickets, and a continueUrl — the link the user opens to finish the listing on tixel.com. If isPending is true the email hasn't been read yet; wait a moment and call again with the same sessionToken. A status of "parsed", "ai_accepted", "links_sent" or "listed" means the tickets were recognised and continueUrl is ready; "parsing_error" or "ignored" means it couldn't be used.

Use after reading a user-provided statement, PDF, or described transactions — not to correct existing rows (use edit_transaction for that, or delete + recreate for direction flips). Groups lines under one operation; cashflow is attributed to operation_date month, not today. Send whole statements in one call with expected_count set; the response lists saved and not_saved rows — if ok is false, check not_saved, fix ONLY those rows, and resend ONLY them. Each edit is committed independently (partial success is possible) — the results array states the outcome per item; retry only items with ok=false. tools_if_shown.name: searchAxiomDocs
tools_if_shown.description: Search official Axiom documentation and return the top matching pages as Markdown with source URLs. Use when you need current product details, unfamiliar APL/MPL syntax, troubleshooting guidance, or requested documentation. Use specific keywords to narrow results. Reuse relevant pages already in context and cite their URLs when relying on them. Call readAxiomDoc with a known page path or a linked .md URL to read another page. Each page defaults to a 12,000-character excerpt; set truncate: false to read the complete fetched pages.

Use searchAxiomDocs when you do not know the page path. Reuse relevant pages already in context and cite the source URL when relying on this page. Pages default to a 12,000-character excerpt; set truncate: false to read the complete fetched page.

tools_if_shown.name: listOrganizations
tools_if_shown.description: List organizations the current credentials can access. Use an id as orgId on other tools to override the session's default organization.

tools_if_shown.name: listDatasets
tools_if_shown.description:
List all available datasets with exact, unquoted names. Tools by dataset kind:
- events / otel.traces / other: getDatasetFields() for fields (set includeMetadata: true for dataset metadata); queryDataset() for APL queries; runSpotlight() for differences between event populations, with automatic field discovery or an explicit field list.
- otel:metrics:v1 / otel-metrics-v1: getDatasetFields({ datasetName, includeMetadata: true }) for dataset metadata; listMetrics(), queryMetrics(), searchMetrics(), listMetricTags(), and getMetricTagValues() for metrics. queryDataset() and runSpotlight() do not support metrics.

Datasets with the same "correlationGroup" are linked for cross-signal investigation (logs, traces, metrics). When investigating one dataset, query the others listed under the same group in correlation-groups.csv below.

tools_if_shown.name: createDataset
tools_if_shown.description:
Create a new dataset in the current organization (POST /v2/datasets). Use this when the user asks to create a dataset or when a needed dataset does not exist yet. Does not create API tokens.

Kinds (optional `kind`, defaults to axiom:events:v1) — same two options as the Axiom Console:
- axiom:events:v1 (Events) — logs or traces; getDatasetFields() for fields, queryDataset() for APL queries.
- otel:metrics:v1 (Metrics) — OTel metrics; getDatasetFields({ datasetName, includeMetadata: true }) for dataset metadata, listMetrics() and queryMetrics() for metrics.

Optional `retentionDays`: custom retention period in days. Omit to use the organization default. Subject to plan limits.

Dataset names must be 1-80 characters, start and end with a letter or number, and may contain letters, numbers, underscores, dots, and hyphens. Ingest requires a separate API token created in the Axiom UI.

tools_if_shown.name: getDatasetFields
tools_if_shown.description: Get observed field names, types, and descriptions as CSV for an events or traces dataset. Set includeMetadata: true to also return complete dataset metadata. Metadata and guidance are compact JSON. Metrics datasets return guidance instead of fields; for metric definitions and dimensions, use listMetrics() and listMetricTags().

tools_if_shown.name: queryDataset
tools_if_shown.description:
# Instructions
1. Query Axiom datasets using Axiom Processing Language (APL). The query must be a valid APL query string.
   For comparative investigations, use runSpotlight() to discover distinguishing dimensions or investigate a shortlist; it handles field eligibility and query batching. Use queryDataset() to verify leads with focused counts and rates, or to write a custom comparison.
   **Only use this for `events`, `otel.traces`, and similar datasets. Do NOT use for `otel-metrics-v1` datasets — use `queryMetrics()` instead.**
2. ALWAYS understand schema before substantive queries—do not guess column names or types. Prefer `getDatasetFields()` or APL
    `| where _time > ago(5m) | getschema` on a narrow window (use dataset names from `listDatasets`); use `take 1` or project specific columns for sample values.
    Before you `where` or `summarize` by a field, estimate cardinality on recent data: `| where _time > ago(5m) | summarize count() by <field> | top 10 by count_`.
    Avoid `project *` or projecting all fields on very wide datasets unless deliberately mapping shape (see item 5). Skipping probes causes wrong field names, bad types, and expensive re-runs.
3. Keep in mind that there's a maximum row limit of 65000 rows per query.
4. Prefer aggregations over non aggregating queries when possible to reduce the amount of data returned.
5. Be selective in what you project in each query (unless otherwise needed, like for discovering the schema). It's expensive to project all fields.
6. ALWAYS restrict `startTime`/`endTime` to the narrowest window that answers the question—every query scans data and consumes resources.
    Prefer the smallest APL per step; widen time or complexity only after probing (item 2).
7. When filtering for a specific term or value, put it on the right field—use `has`/`has_cs`/`contains` there after item 2. See **Avoid `search`** under Query performance rules.
8. **`map[string]` columns (e.g. `attributes`, `attributes.custom`, `resource` in OTel-style data)** — `getDatasetFields` and
    in-query `getschema` show the type but **not** the keys inside the map. You must **sample** (`take`, `project` the map
    column, or `mv-expand` + `summarize` to list keys) to learn the structure, then use bracket access
    (e.g. `['attributes']['http.method']`, `['attributes.custom']['http.response.status_code']`). Do not assume key names
    across services or SDK versions.
9. Query cost limits may apply to your credentials. When configured, each result ends with a budget footer (query cost and remaining hourly/daily budget, in GB-hours — GBhr, the unit limits are enforced in) — heed its warnings.
    Exceeding a limit rejects further queries until the window resets (fixed UTC hour/day boundaries); the error says when.
10. Use searchAxiomDocs() or readAxiomDoc() to verify unfamiliar APL operators, functions, or product behavior before querying.

### Query performance rules

1. **Narrow `startTime`/`endTime`** — These bound how much data is scanned. Do not rely on in-query `_time` filters alone; keep the API window as tight as your question allows.
2. **`_time` first in APL** — When you filter on `_time` in the query text, put `where _time between (...)` before other filters. This keeps extra in-query narrowing fast.
3. **Most selective `where` first** — Axiom does not reorder predicates; put the filter that removes the most rows earliest.
4. **`project` early and narrowly** — Avoid pulling all columns from very wide datasets (expensive payloads; risk of failures on huge rows).
5. **Prefer fast string ops** — Use `_cs` (case-sensitive) variants when possible; prefer `startswith`/`endswith` over `contains` when applicable; `matches regex` only as a last resort.
6. **Use `has`/`has_cs` for unique-looking strings** — IDs, UUIDs, trace IDs, error codes, session tokens. `has` leverages full-text indexes when available and is much faster than `contains` for high-entropy terms. Use `contains` only when you need true substring matching (e.g., partial paths).
7. **Duration literals** — e.g. `duration > 10s`, not manual conversion.
8. **Avoid search** — scans ALL fields. Use `has`/`has_cs`/`contains` on specific fields.
9. **Avoid heavy `parse_json()` in hot paths** — Filter/narrow first when possible.
10. **Avoid pack(*)** — creates dict of ALL fields per row. Use pack with named fields only.
11. Limit results—use take 10 or top 20 instead of default 1000 when exploring.
12. **Field quoting**—quote identifiers with dots/dashes/spaces: ['geo.country']. For map field keys, use index notation: ['attributes.custom']['http.protocol'].

# Examples
Basic:
- Filter: ['logs'] | where ['severity'] == "error" or ['duration'] > 500ms
- Time range: ['logs'] | where ['_time'] > ago(2h) and ['_time'] < now()
- Project rename: ['logs'] | project-rename responseTime=['duration'], path=['url']

Aggregations:
- Count by: ['logs'] | summarize count() by bin(['_time'], 5m), ['status']
- Multiple aggs: ['logs'] | summarize count(), avg(['duration']), max(['duration']), p95=percentile(['duration'], 95) by ['endpoint']
- Compare populations: use runSpotlight() for discovery and focused comparisons; for custom APL, ['logs'] | summarize spotlight(['isError'], ['endpoint'])
- Histograms: ['logs'] | summarize histogram(['responseTime'], 100) by ['endpoint']
- Distinct: ['logs'] | summarize dcount(['userId']) by bin_auto(['_time'])

Text matching & Parse:
- Match on known fields (avoid full-row `search`): ['logs'] | where ['message'] has_cs "error" or ['message'] has_cs "exception"
- Parse logs: ['logs'] | parse-kv ['message'] as (duration:long, error:string) with (pair_delimiter=",")
- Regex extract: ['logs'] | extend errorCode = extract("error code ([0-9]+)", 1, ['message'])
- Contains ops: ['logs'] | where ['message'] contains_cs "ERROR" or ['message'] startswith "FATAL"

Data Shaping:
- Extend & Calculate: ['logs'] | extend duration_s = ['duration']/1000, success = ['status'] < 400
- Dynamic: ['logs'] | extend props = parse_json(['properties']) | where ['props.level'] == "error"
- Pack/Unpack: ['logs'] | extend fields = pack("status", ['status'], "duration", ['duration'])
- Arrays: ['logs'] | where ['url'] in ("login", "logout", "home") | where array_length(['tags']) > 0

Advanced:
- Union: union ['logs-app*'] | where ['severity'] == "error"
- Case: ['logs'] | extend level = case(['status'] >= 500, "error", ['status'] >= 400, "warn", "info")

Time Operations:
- Bin & Range: ['logs'] | where ['_time'] between(datetime(2024-01-01)..now())
- Multiple time bins: ['logs'] | summarize count() by bin(['_time'], 1h), bin(['_time'], 1d)
- Time shifts: ['logs'] | extend prev_hour = ['_time'] - 1h

String Operations:
- String funcs: ['logs'] | extend domain = tolower(extract("://([^/]+)", 1, ['url']))
- Concat: ['logs'] | extend full_msg = strcat(['level'], ": ", ['message'])
- Replace: ['logs'] | extend clean_msg = replace_regex("(password=)[^&]*", "\1***", ['message'])

Common Patterns:
- Error analysis: ['logs'] | where ['severity'] == "error" | summarize error_count=count() by ['error_code'], ['service']
- Status codes: ['logs'] | summarize requests=count() by ['status'], bin_auto(['_time']) | where ['status'] >= 500
- Latency tracking: ['logs'] | summarize p50=percentile(['duration'], 50), p90=percentile(['duration'], 90) by ['endpoint']
- User activity: ['logs'] | summarize user_actions=count() by ['userId'], ['action'], bin(['_time'], 1h)

tools_if_shown.name: runSpotlight
tools_if_shown.description:
Use the APL spotlight() aggregation to find dimensions that distinguish a comparison population from its baseline. Use for "what changed?", slow versus normal requests, or errors versus successful requests after identifying a dataset and focused time scope.
Provide datasetName, fixed startTime/endTime, and an APL scalar boolean predicate: true=comparison, false=baseline, null=excluded. Bounds are start inclusive and end exclusive. For a comparison between time intervals, use a predicate over _time and bounds covering both populations. Optional filter applies to both populations. Use fixed RFC3339 timestamps with at most millisecond precision. Expressions cannot contain pipelines, statements, comments, raw/prefixed/adjacent strings, now(), or ago().
Omit fields to explore all eligible dimensions without enumerating the schema yourself; supply exact field names when you already have a shortlist. Both paths read the dataset schema and apply the same eligibility checks. The tool excludes maps, arrays, system time fields, and direct predicate references, quotes identifiers, counts both cohorts once, and runs sequential batches of at most 50 dimensions. Inspect indirect references yourself. It separates null-only and empty typed populations into insufficientData before ranking comparable findings. Each list is independently bounded by limit, with separate totals and omission counts. Categorical values are ordered by combined baseline/comparison frequency, then absolute frequency change, bounded by valueLimit. Prefer relevant dimensions over IDs/free text when narrowing an investigation.
Returns precise JSON typed statistics, raw dimensions plus schema-matched fieldName for reuse in fields, cohort counts, excluded fields, generated APL, diagnostics, query budgets, and coverage of completed/pending fields. Empty cohorts stop after counting. Before each batch, a budget header reporting zero remaining stops the next query. Missing headers do not establish exhaustion. A failed/partial/estimated batch stops execution; findings from completed batches remain available with incomplete coverage. Fixed bounds do not freeze ingestion between queries.
delta_score only ranks leads; scores, p-values, and normalized ratios are not causal confidence or ordinary percent changes. Validate leads with queryDataset counts/rates and an independent window. For otel:metrics:v1 datasets use the metrics tools.

tools_if_shown.name: queryMetrics
tools_if_shown.description:
# Instructions
1. Query OpenTelemetry metrics stored in Axiom using MPL (Metrics Processing Language). NOT APL.
2. The query targets a metrics dataset (kind "otel-metrics-v1").
3. Use listMetrics() to discover available metric names and inspect metric type, temporality, and unit before querying whenever query semantics matter.
4. Use listMetricTags() and getMetricTagValues() with metricName to discover filtering dimensions for the metric you will query.
5. ALWAYS restrict the time range to the smallest possible range that meets your needs.
6. NEVER guess metric names or tag values. Always discover them first.
7. Query cost limits may apply to your credentials. When configured, each result ends with a budget footer (query cost and remaining hourly/daily budget, in GB-hours — GBhr, the unit limits are enforced in) — heed its warnings.
   Exceeding a limit rejects further queries until the window resets (fixed UTC hour/day boundaries); the error says when.
8. Use getMetricsSpec({ datasetName }) for current MPL syntax, functions, and examples before writing unfamiliar queries. Use searchAxiomDocs() or readAxiomDoc() for additional metric semantics or product behavior.
9. Results include query metadata as compact JSON before the series. Heed backend warnings and preserve the order of group_keys when interpreting groups. custom_unit overrides unit; when ignore_unit is true, only custom_unit applies, if supplied. Do not infer a unit when none applies. Metadata describes the returned values; do not rescale them just to apply a unit label.

# MPL Query Syntax
A query has three parts: source, filtering, and transformation. Filters must appear before transformations.

## Source
```
<dataset>:<metric>
```
Backtick-escape identifiers containing special characters: ``my-dataset``:``http.server.duration``

## Filtering (where)
Chain filters with `|`. Use `where` (not `filter`, which is deprecated).
```
| where <tag> <op> <value>
```
Operators: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=
Values: "string", 42, 42.0, true, /regexp/
Combine with: and, or, not, parentheses

## Transformations

### Aggregation (align) — aggregate data over time windows
```
| align to <interval> using <function>
```
Functions: avg, sum, min, max, count, last
Intervals: 5m, 1h, 1d, etc.

### Grouping (group) — group series by tags
```
| group by <tag1>, <tag2> using <function>
```
Functions: avg, sum, min, max, count
Without `by`: combines all series: `| group using sum`

### Mapping (map) — transform values in place
```
| map rate                    // per-second rate of change
| map increase                // increase between datapoints
| map + 5                     // arithmetic: +, -, *, /
| map abs                     // absolute value
| map fill::prev              // fill gaps with previous value
| map fill::const(0)          // fill gaps with constant
| map filter::lt(0.4)         // remove datapoints >= 0.4
| map filter::gt(100)         // remove datapoints <= 100
| map is::gte(0.5)            // set to 1.0 if >= 0.5, else 0.0
```

### Computation (compute) — combine two metrics
```
(
  `dataset`:`errors_total` | group using sum,
  `dataset`:`requests_total` | group using sum;
)
| compute error_rate using /
```
Functions: +, -, *, /, min, max, avg

### Bucketing (bucket) — for histograms
```
| bucket by method, path to 5m using histogram(count, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99)
| bucket by method to 5m using interpolate_delta_histogram(0.90, 0.99)
| bucket by method to 5m using interpolate_cumulative_histogram(rate, 0.90, 0.99)
```

### Prometheus compatibility
```
| align to 5m using prom::rate   // Prometheus-style rate
```

## Identifiers
Use backticks for names with special characters: ``my-dataset``, ``service.name``, ``http.request.duration``

# Query Planning With Metric Definitions
Inspect the `type` and `temporality` fields returned by listMetrics() before choosing query strategy. Treat the following as guidance rather than strict rules, and prioritize the user's intent when appropriate.

- If `type` is `Gauge`, use current values or an aggregation appropriate to the question; do not apply a rate unless the user asks for the change in that gauge.

- If `type` is `CounterNonMonotonic`, clarify whether the user wants its current value or its change over time before choosing a rate or delta.

- If `type` is `CounterMonotonic` and `temporality` is `cumulative`, treat it as a cumulative counter. `rate`, `prom::rate`, or `increase` are often more appropriate than raw values for questions about changes over time.

- If `type` is `CounterMonotonic` and `temporality` is `delta`, treat samples as per-collection-interval increments, not instantaneous gauge values.

- If `type` is `Histogram`, use bucket functions for count, average, sum, and percentile queries. Choose `interpolate_delta_histogram(...)` for delta temporality and `interpolate_cumulative_histogram(...)` for cumulative temporality.

- If `type` is `Summary`, do not treat it like histogram buckets.

- If `type` or `temporality` is missing or ambiguous, generate the most conservative query and explicitly note any assumptions.

# Parameters and Chart Resolution
Bind declared MPL parameters using bare names and MPL literal values: `params: { svc: '"frontend"', window: '5m' }` (no `$` or `param__` prefix).

Optional `chartWidth` and `pixelPerPoint` guide automatic `$__interval` resolution; fixed intervals such as `5m` are unchanged.

# Examples
Basic query:
  `my-metrics`:`http.server.duration` | align to 5m using avg

Filtered:
  `my-metrics`:`http.server.duration` | where `service.name` == "frontend" | align to 5m using avg

Grouped:
  `my-metrics`:`http.server.duration` | align to 5m using avg | group by endpoint using sum

Rate:
  `my-metrics`:`http.requests.total` | align to 5m using prom::rate | group by method, path, code using sum

Error rate (compute):
  (
    `my-metrics`:`http.requests.total` | where code >= 400 | group by method, path using sum,
    `my-metrics`:`http.requests.total` | group by method, path using sum;
  )
  | compute error_rate using /
  | align to 5m using avg

SLI (error budget):
  (
    `my-metrics`:`http.requests.total` | where code >= 500 | align to 1h using prom::rate | group using sum,
    `my-metrics`:`http.requests.total` | align to 1h using prom::rate | group using sum;
  )
  | compute error_rate using /
  | map is::lt(0.2)
  | align to 7d using avg

Set truncate: false to return the complete metrics-v2 JSON in structuredContent and text, including every series, sample, summary, tag, and metadata field received from the backend. Use structuredContent when saving results for charts or other programs; the text can include a query-budget footer.

Histogram percentiles:
  `my-metrics`:`http.request.duration.seconds.bucket` | bucket by method, path to 5m using interpolate_delta_histogram(0.90, 0.99)

Fill gaps:
  `my-metrics`:`cpu.usage` | map fill::prev | align to 1m using avg

tools_if_shown.name: listMetrics
tools_if_shown.description: List metric names, types, temporality, and units as CSV in a metrics dataset (kind "otel-metrics-v1"). Start here when query semantics matter to choose between avg, rate, increase, histogram bucketing, and related query strategies.

tools_if_shown.name: listMetricTags
tools_if_shown.description: List available tags (dimensions) as one-column CSV in a metrics dataset (kind `otel-metrics-v1`). Supply metricName from listMetrics or searchMetrics to discover tags for that specific metric; omit it to list tags across the dataset. Tags can be used to filter and group metrics queries.

tools_if_shown.name: searchMetrics
tools_if_shown.description:
Start here when the user mentions a specific service, host, or entity name and you need to work with metrics data.

Searches tag values across all metrics in a dataset and returns the metric names that are associated with the given entity. This is the fastest way to go from a known entity name (e.g. "checkout-service", "api-gateway", "us-east-1") to a concrete list of metric names you can actually query.

Returns CSV with metric name, matched tags, type, temporality, and unit. The matchedTags cell contains a JSON array of tag names.

**Time range:** Use a window of at least 3 hours. Recently-ingested data can take up to 2 hours to become searchable here, so narrow windows may return empty results even when data exists. For recent data, default to `now-3h` / `now`. For historical data, use whatever window covers the period you care about — e.g. `now-14d` / `now-7d` is valid.

**Workflow:**
1. Call this tool with the entity name to get relevant metric names.
2. Use listMetricTags() / getMetricTagValues() with metricName to discover filter dimensions for a specific matching metric.
3. Call queryMetrics() with an MPL query targeting the specific metric and filters.

Use listMetrics() instead when you have no entity name to search by and need a full catalogue of what's in the dataset.

tools_if_shown.name: getMetricTagValues
tools_if_shown.description: List values for a tag as one-column CSV in a metrics dataset (kind `otel-metrics-v1`). Supply metricName from listMetrics or searchMetrics to discover values for that specific metric and tag; omit it to list values across the dataset. Useful for discovering filter values before querying.

tools_if_shown.name: sendFeedback
tools_if_shown.description:
Share feedback about your experience with the Axiom MCP server. Use this when:
- A tool description was misleading, unclear, or led you to call the wrong tool
- A tool result or error message was confusing, unhelpful, or hard to parse
- A capability you needed was missing
- Something worked particularly well and should not change

IMPORTANT: Never include sensitive information. Do not include log or query contents, dataset values, credentials, API tokens, personal data, or anything else from the user's environment or conversation. Describe the issue generically — e.g. "the startTime default on queryDataset was unclear", not actual query results. Feedback is stored and reviewed by the Axiom team.

tools_if_shown.name: services-getMap
tools_if_shown.description: START HERE for any question about service topology, dependencies, or system-wide health. Returns the whole service dependency graph Stitch observed, in one call — every edge (service→service, database, messaging, external) with call volume, error rate and approximate p50/p99 — so no discovery ladder is needed: do not list services or operations first, just call this. Every edge carries a confidence value qualifying how the dependency was established: `confirmed_*` edges come from directly linked spans and can be trusted as real, `inferred_*` edges were reconstructed heuristically and should be treated as hypotheses to verify. Rows with an empty `dst` are node rows — a service's own request-handling metrics, not a dependency. Exemplar trace ids are returned for erroring and unusually slow edges so you can jump straight to a trace; use services-getChanges for what changed recently (new or disappeared dependencies, p99 regressions), and services-getEdgeHistory once you have a suspect edge, to see when it regressed and whether the shape is a deploy-like step or a gradual drift. Pass `view: "services"` for one row per service — call volume, error rate, latency and dependency counts — when the question is which service is unhealthy rather than which dependency.

tools_if_shown.name: services-getChanges
tools_if_shown.description: Report what changed in the service dependency graph: dependencies that appeared, dependencies that disappeared, and edges whose p99 latency regressed against a trailing 6h baseline. Every kind sits behind conservative volume and confidence gates, so silence here means nothing crossed the bar rather than nothing was checked. Novelty is suppressed when the rollup does not reach back past the novelty window, because a fresh dataset or short retention would make every edge look new. Use services-getMap for the current shape of the graph; this tool only answers what moved.

tools_if_shown.name: services-getEdgeHistory
tools_if_shown.description: Charts one service's edges over time: a per-bucket time series of calls, errors and approximate p50/p99 for every edge where the named service is the source or the destination (pass `dst` to narrow to a single directed edge). Use it after services-getMap flags a slow or erroring edge, to answer when it got slow and whether the shape is a step — deploy-shaped, a jump between two adjacent buckets — or a gradual drift, and to find the bucket where it started. This tool reports raw per-bucket numbers with no gating: use services-getMap for the whole graph as it stands now, and services-getChanges for gated change detection (new or disappeared dependencies, p99 regressions that clear the volume gates).

detail_provenance.offline_parser_correction: Decoded escaped leading dollar literals and omitted Flight undefined properties; original HTML hash/timestamp retained.

published_auth_text: commercetools knowledge does not require authentication. It is a public MCP endpoint you can connect without logging in.
